title: Beware Sharpe Ratios for Private Markets | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional's Wes Crill argues Sharpe ratios are unreliable for private market strategies because stale NAV-based pricing understates volatility, illustrated by publicly traded BDCs showing 13.4% annualized quarterly-return volatility over five years versus just 2.7% for nontraded BDCs holding largely the same underlying assets.

themes.theme: Sharpe Ratio Interpretation Breaks Down for Nontraded Assets

insights.claim: The Sharpe ratio is often interpreted as a measure of how much return an investor gets per unit of risk, but this interpretation only holds if the return volatility used in the calculation actually captures real-time changes in the underlying asset's value.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Investors comparing Sharpe ratios across public and private strategies should first check whether the volatility inputs are even measuring the same thing.
insights.quote: as a measure of how much return you get per unit of risk

insights.claim: Public markets let assets trade at continuously updated prices, so changes in fair value are reflected instantaneously in price movements, whereas nontraded assets have no real-time value indicator and instead report returns based on periodically updated net asset values (NAVs) that can be stale.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Stale NAV pricing mechanically suppresses measured volatility for private holdings, which will make any Sharpe-ratio-based risk comparison to public markets misleading.
insights.quote: Nontraded assets, on the other hand, don’t have real-time indicators of their value.
insights.locator: Public markets allow assets to trade

themes.theme: BDC Case Study: Listed vs. Nonlisted Volatility Gap

insights.claim: Over the past five years, the annualized standard deviation of quarterly returns was 13.4% for publicly traded business development companies (BDCs) versus just 2.7% for nontraded BDCs.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: A roughly 5x gap in reported volatility between listed and nonlisted vehicles holding similar assets shows the scale of understatement investors should adjust for when using Sharpe ratios on private credit funds.
insights.quote: The annualized standard deviation of quarterly returns over the past five years was 13.4% for publicly traded BDCs versus just 2.7% for nontraded BDCs.
insights.locator: The difference in volatility is not subtle

insights.claim: Indices of traded BDCs are sometimes used as a public proxy for private credit because these companies primarily purchase private credit debt, making the listed-versus-nonlisted BDC comparison a useful natural experiment for how pricing mechanisms affect measured risk in private credit.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Analysts using listed BDC indices as a private credit proxy should be aware the comparison set (nonlisted BDCs) reports artificially smooth returns.
insights.locator: As we have written in the past

insights.claim: Nonlisted BDCs are not exchange-traded and therefore lack a mechanism to incorporate the market's views in real time, unlike listed BDCs whose prices change continuously based on market views.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The absence of a real-time pricing mechanism is the direct cause of the volatility gap, not any underlying difference in economic risk.
insights.quote: Nonlisted BDCs, on the other hand, are not exchange-traded and therefore lack a mechanism to incorporate the market’s views in real time.
insights.locator: Prices of listed BDCs change continuously

insights.claim: The large volatility gap between listed and nonlisted BDCs exists despite the fact that the underlying investments are often the same between the two classes of BDCs, meaning the difference is a measurement artifact rather than a real difference in economic risk.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Investors should not treat a low reported volatility figure for a nontraded vehicle as evidence of genuinely lower risk if the underlying holdings mirror a much more volatile listed counterpart.
insights.quote: And this is despite the fact that the underlying investments are often the same between the two classes of BDCs.
insights.locator: The difference in volatility is not subtle

themes.theme: Implications for Evaluating Private Market Strategies

insights.claim: The BDC volatility comparison demonstrates the broader challenge in making sense of Sharpe ratios calculated for private market strategies, implying such ratios should not be taken at face value or compared directly against public-market Sharpe ratios.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Allocators evaluating private credit, private equity, or other nontraded strategies on a risk-adjusted basis should discount reported Sharpe ratios or seek volatility measures that correct for stale NAV pricing before comparing them to public benchmarks.
insights.quote: This demonstrates the challenge in making sense out of Sharpe ratios calculated for private market strategies.

source_meta.author: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
